newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Argentine soccer fans run violent rackets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Argentine soccer fans run violent rackets.

text.p: When Argentine soccer fan "Bighead" Sergio's girlfriend got tired of his beatings and shot him to death, police found among his belongings a check he had extorted from his favourite team as a legacy of his thuggish life.

Then they paid a visit to the offices of local club Rosario Central, a traditionally big name in Argentina's first division, to ask why its top officials had signed the $500 check made out to Bighead. The answer had long been one of Argentine soccer's worst-kept secrets.

In enterprising contrast to their better known European counterparts, who employ their energies beating each other senseless, Argentina's own brand of soccer hooligans prefer to run protection rackets bleeding money from their own clubs. In Argentina they are known as "Barra Brava," which translates roughly as "Wild Bunch," and Bighead played a starring role in Rosario's Barra before he was killed late last year.
Bighead and his friends would come barging in to Rosario Central's clubhouse to ask officials for contributions so they could travel to support the team at games out of town.
"They came round here, they said they had to travel, that they wanted money for this, money for that," Rosario Central office manager Roberto Martinez told Reuters.
The consequences of not paying up were clear. "You could tell by the look of them what was going to happen to you," Martinez recalled.
NO THREAT TOO TAME

When Rosario Central treasurer Roberto Munoz was away in Buenos Aires, a group of hooligans threatened to rape and murder his teenage daughter. A tall, heavy-set man, Munoz had annoyed Rosario Central's rougher fans by refusing to hand over cash when they staged their fund-raising stampedes through the club offices.
"I was tough. But then another official would come along and give in and give them money," Munoz said, "So I was the bad guy and the others were the good guys."
It was not just a matter of a few pesos for a bus trip. Munoz worked out that the club was handing over as much as $200,000 a year in cash, free game tickets and fares to a small group of toughs.

The hooligans made even more money as they rarely used the free tickets themselves but sold them instead. "They enter the stadium anyway because they know someone at the gate or they just push their way in," Munoz said.

Everyone who has ever been to a big match in this soccer obsessed country has seen the Barra Brava. Those foolish enough to choose a seat beneath the "popular" stand have probably been spat on by them too.

Some fans take raincoats to matches in the hot Argentine summer and stoically pay no attention when the Barra while away boring patches of play by sending great gobs of spittel swishing down on the seats below. Sometimes a livelier wit will urinate into a plastic bag and lob that down too.
POLICE LOOK ON
Police, who rarely dare to intervene unless it looks like someone is about to get killed, mainly look on good naturedly.

Club officials admit they may have created the problem themselves. It is common knowledge many Barras get paid to turn up at a match to chant in favour of their team, or for or against a player, and to beat drums to whip up the crowd.
Rosario Central is now getting tough on the hooligans after the bad publicity. They have two policemen permanently outside their clubhouse during office hours.

But team officials were not alone in being threatened by their fans, just unusual in admitting it. Most in the game prefer to keep quiet, siphoning off a little of soccer's vast earnings to keep the Barra happy. Only occasionally does the ugly truth break the surface.

The Argentine national team's tough coach Daniel Passarella punched one fan who came pestering him for money when he was working for River Plate in the early 1990s. More recently, Oscar Ruggieri, one of Argentina's most successful soccer players of recent times, admitted paying off the Barra.

One of the few alleged soccer hooligans to be in prison is the most notorious, Jose Barritta, better known as "Grandad." The beer-bellied Barritta is now being tried on charges of running a hooligan mafia living off Boca Juniors, Argentina's most popular club, from the rough docklands of Buenos Aires.

Grandad and eight of his suspected underlings were arrested after a Boca gang ambushed River Plate supporters with guns, killing two, in April 1994. Grandad further embellished his already colourful reputation during a long stretch on the run from police, on one occasion being photographed in the stands watching Boca Juniors.
Barritta's lawyer says his client is innocent of all charges and earned his money working with his mother.
